Understanding International Law in U.S. Courts
International law comprises treaties, customs, and principles that govern relations between countries. While primarily the domain of foreign policy, international law increasingly finds its way into U.S. court rulings, influencing decisions on trade, human rights, and jurisdictional matters.
U.S. courts may refer to international law when federal statutes incorporate international obligations or when interpreting ambiguous domestic laws. This integration ensures consistency with global norms while safeguarding national interests.

How U.S. Courts Apply International Law
U.S. courts apply international law in various contexts, including treaty enforcement, customary international law recognition, and resolving conflicts with domestic laws. The Supreme Court and lower courts carefully analyze international agreements to interpret their scope and applicability.
Additionally, courts consider international human rights treaties in cases involving civil liberties and immigration. Though international law is not always binding domestically without congressional approval, it serves as persuasive authority guiding judicial reasoning.

Key Cases Demonstrating International Law Influence
Landmark rulings such as Medellín v. Texas highlight the complex relationship between international law and U.S. courts. The case involved the enforcement of a judgment from the International Court of Justice, underscoring the limits of treaty enforcement without congressional action.

 Peruvian Court Halts $17 Million Money Laundering Case Against Fujimori

 
 
 By Juan Martinez
 ·

 ·

 A Peruvian court’s decision to dismiss the high-profile money laundering trial against Keiko Fujimori has sent shockwaves through the nation’s political sphere. The ruling, announced on January 13, 2025, effectively halts proceedings against the three-time presidential candidate and daughter of former President Alberto Fujimori.
Judge Mercedes Caballero cited procedural flaws in the indictment as the reason for the dismissal. The trial, which began in 2024, accused Fujimori of receiving approximately $17 million in illegal funds from Brazilian construction giant Odebrecht and other entities to finance her 2011 and 2016 presidential campaigns.
This legal development carries significant implications for Peru’s political future.
